claims.text: The starting material is a nanoscale multilayer HEA coating with alternating FCC and BCC layers.
The starting multilayer is uniform and initially scarce in defects and pre-existing dislocation sources.
Sustained loading will be applied through nanoindentation creep while deformation is observed by in situ TEM.
The tests will be conducted at room temperature with controlled loading rates and nanoscale layer thicknesses.
Sustained loading causes elastic undulations to develop at the multilayer interfaces.
The interfacial elastic undulations have a characteristic wavelength of approximately 1–2 nm.
Coherent multilayer interfaces possess an intrinsic elastic instability responsible for progressive undulation growth.
Interfacial undulations locally amplify stress concentrations.
The stress concentrations generated by undulations facilitate dislocation nucleation at interfaces.
Sequential dislocation nucleation and accumulation produce a gradual transition from elastic to plastic deformation.
HEA structural complexity can promote extensive dislocation nucleation during the elastic-to-plastic transition.
Interfacial undulations should appear before and spatially correlate with dislocation-nucleation events.
Nanoindentation creep curves should show a transition from primarily elastic response to localized interfacial dislocation nucleation.
The proposed behavior contrasts with a homogeneous plastic-deformation profile.
The mechanism should be more pronounced when interface integrity and coherence are maintained.
The mechanism is expected to dominate for nanoscale multilayer spacings, exemplified as less than 100 nm.
Increasing the layer thickness can overwhelm the interface-induced mechanism.
Diffusive mechanisms at elevated temperature can overwhelm the interface-induced mechanism.
Very high loading rates can cause the interface-induced mechanism to be overwhelmed.
The hypothesis is falsified if interface-specific undulations are absent or if dislocation nucleation is spatially uncorrelated with them.
